title: Highway 1090 Mae Sot–Umphang 2026: The 1,219-Curve Road | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A driving guide to Highway 1090 from Mae Sot to Umphang in Tak, Thailand — the 1,219-curve mountain road over 164 km. Real stops at Tharn Rak and Pha Charoen waterfalls, valley viewpoints, Mae Klong coffee market, plus safe mountain-driving tips.
keywords: Highway 1090, 1219 curves road, Mae Sot Umphang, sky highway Thailand, road trip Tak, things to do Tak
intro: Highway 1090 from Mae Sot to Umphang is the road locals in Tak call the 1,219-curve road — 164 kilometres that wind along the ridgeline the whole way, the kind of drive a lot of people never forget. It's tiring and beautiful in roughly equal measure. This is a friend-to-friend rundown of what the road is actually like to drive, where you can stop, where the valley viewpoints are, and how to prepare so it's fun rather than nerve-wracking.
chips: ⛰️ Ridgeline valley views, Thanon Thong Chai range

blocks.html: First, understand that 1090 isn't a road you just drive through — the road itself is the experience. It was built to follow the Thanon Thong Chai mountain range that marks the Thailand–Myanmar border, and the whole route is a narrow two-lane road climbing and dropping without a break. Nearly everyone who drives it for the first time says the same thing: it's more tiring than the kilometre count suggests. But once you see the ridgelines stacked up in layers, you understand why people put themselves through it.

The road has another name that foreigners use — the Death Highway. It sounds frightening, but the real reason behind it has nothing to do with how dangerous the road is today. It comes from a tragedy that happened while the road was being built decades ago. These days, if you drive slowly, stay alert, and bring a car that's in good shape, the road isn't as scary as its nickname. That said, you can't let your guard down, because the curves really do come one after another.

blocks.text: What the 1,219-curve road is, and what it's like to drive

blocks.html: The figure of 1,219 curves isn't marketing — it's the number of bends actually counted along the 164-kilometre route from Mae Sot to Umphang. In Umphang town there's even a sign with the number for people to photograph as a keepsake. The first 20 kilometres out of Mae Sot are still flat, hugging the Moei River, and easy to drive. After that the road starts climbing into the mountains and snakes up and down the ridgeline all the way to the end.

items: Distance — about 164 kilometres, but don't go by the number, because it's mountain road the whole way
Driving time — at least 4 hours without stops; with photo breaks and rest stops, plan for 5–6 hours
Road condition — paved the whole way, two lanes, narrow shoulders, few roadside pull-offs
Gearing — a regular sedan can handle it if it's in good shape; you'll need low gear to help brake on the long descents

blocks.title: Check before you set off
blocks.html: Brakes and tyres are the two things to be most sure about before tackling this road, because there are several long descents — weak brakes make it tiring and risky. Fill up the tank completely back in Mae Sot, since fuel stations along the way are few and far apart.

blocks.text: Stops along the way, by the kilometre marker

blocks.html: The charm of 1090 is that there's something to stop for the whole way, especially in the first half out of Mae Sot — mostly pretty limestone waterfalls and viewpoints. Going by the kilometre markers, here's roughly what you'll find.

items.name: Tharn Rak Waterfall (around km 26)
items.blurb: A roadside waterfall pouring down a tall rock cliff, with a golden chedi perched on the cliff above it. A good spot to stop for photos and stretch your legs before the road starts curving hard. It's on the left as you come from Mae Sot.

items.name: Pha Charoen Waterfall (around km 37)
items.blurb: The highlight of the early stretch — a limestone waterfall cascading down hundreds of small tiers, which is why people call it the 97-tier waterfall. It sits inside a national park with a restaurant and toilets, making it the main rest stop before the serious curves begin.
items.meta: About 700 m off the main road · main rest stop

items.name: Mid-route valley viewpoint
items.blurb: About 40 kilometres before Umphang, there's a spot where the road opens up to ridgelines stacked in layers reaching all the way to the Myanmar side. Many people call it the most rewarding view on the whole route. On a clear day you can see ranges lined up in ribbons as far as the eye can see.

items.name: Mae Klong Headwaters Market (coffee)
items.blurb: A small coffee shop with snacks in the second half of the route, with toilets and basic essentials. A good place to take a break after a long stretch of curves, just before you reach Umphang town.
items.meta: Second half of the route · coffee break

blocks.title: Where to take your motion-sickness pill
blocks.html: Pha Charoen Waterfall is the best place to take a motion-sickness pill if you're prone to it, because after that the road starts curving hard and doesn't let up. Taking the pill about 20–30 minutes before the curvy section works better than waiting until you start feeling queasy.

blocks.text: Valley views and the most beautiful stretch

blocks.html: If you ask which part of 1090 is the most beautiful, most people give the same answer: the second half, just before Umphang, where the road climbs high onto the ridgeline and opens up views of the valleys on both sides. In some sections it feels like you're driving along the actual spine of the mountain, looking down on green forest and thin mist drifting in the valley — and that's when you understand why they call it the sky highway.

Early morning through late morning is when the views are best, because the sky is still clear and there's a chance of seeing a sea of mist in the valleys. By late afternoon the light flattens out, and some days rain clouds roll in and hide the ridges. That's another reason people recommend leaving Mae Sot early — it's not only about safety, it's about the views too.

items: Morning — clear sky, a chance to see the sea of mist in the high valleys, sharpest views
Late morning — sun lights up the roadside waterfalls, the curtains of water show up clearly
Late afternoon — light flattens, some days rain clouds hide the ridges, and you risk driving in the dark if you start late

blocks.html: Highway 1090 ends at Umphang, the deepest forest district in Tak. Most people who battle the curves all day do it to reach the places out here. If you're planning a trip, treat this road as only half the journey — the real destination needs several more days.

items.name: Thi Lo Su Waterfall
items.blurb: A massive limestone waterfall that many rank as the most beautiful in Thailand. You need a 4WD to get further in from Umphang town, and it's open for visits roughly September to May.

items.name: Doi Hua Mot
items.blurb: A bald-topped hill near Umphang town, a spot for sunrise and a sea of mist in every direction. You can head up from the early hours.

items.name: Mae Klong Headwaters Rafting
items.blurb: Rubber-raft trips past cliffside waterfalls and hot springs deep in the forest, most fun when the water is high in the rainy season.

blocks.text: Driving 1090 safely: tips from people who've been

blocks.html: This road isn't as dangerous as its nickname if you know how to drive and prepare well, but there are a few things people who've been keep stressing. Worth keeping in mind before you set off.

items: Leave early — set off from Mae Sot before 9 a.m. so you reach Umphang before dark, avoiding the curves in the dark and the afternoon rain and mist
Use low gear on descents — don't ride the brakes the whole way down; let engine braking slow you so the brakes don't overheat and fade
Lights on and honk into blind curves — on many bends you can't see oncoming traffic, so switch on your lights and tap the horn as you enter blind corners
Expect to lose signal — mobile signal drops out in patches in the high mountains, so download an offline map beforehand for peace of mind
There are checkpoints — there are several checkpoints along the way since this is a border area; most just wave you through, but keep your ID on you

blocks.title: If you get carsick easily, sit up front
blocks.html: If you're travelling in a group and someone gets carsick easily, put them in the front seat looking far down the road — it's better than sitting in the back. Pack leak-proof plastic bags, a cool towel, and water in the car too. A thousand-plus curves is no joke.

faq.q: How many curves and how long is Highway 1090 from Mae Sot to Umphang?
faq.a: About 1,219 curves over roughly 164 kilometres. It's a two-lane mountain road the whole way. Driving it takes at least 4 hours without stops; with photo breaks and rest stops, plan for 5–6 hours.

faq.q: Can you drive a regular sedan on Highway 1090?
faq.a: Yes, if the car is in good shape and the driver is confident on mountain roads. Check the brakes and tyres carefully before you leave, and use low gear to help slow down on the long descents. It's only the road that continues from Umphang into Thi Lo Su Waterfall that requires a 4WD.

faq.q: Where can you stop along Highway 1090?
faq.a: Early in the route from Mae Sot there's Tharn Rak Waterfall around km 26 and Pha Charoen Waterfall around km 37, the main rest stop with toilets. In the second half there's a valley viewpoint about 40 kilometres before Umphang, and the Mae Klong Headwaters Market for a coffee break.

faq.q: What time should you leave Mae Sot?
faq.a: Before 9 a.m. is best, so you reach Umphang before dark and avoid driving the curves in the dark. The morning sky is also still clear, giving you a chance to see the sea of mist in the valleys, while late afternoon can bring rain clouds that hide the views on some days.

faq.q: Is Highway 1090 really dangerous, and why is it called the Death Highway?
faq.a: The name Death Highway comes from a tragedy that happened while the road was being built decades ago — it has nothing to do with how dangerous the road is today. If you drive slowly, stay alert, prepare your car well, and leave early, this road is safe to drive. Still, you can't be careless, because the curves really do come back to back.
